# Cut scores, reporting and communicating results {#reporting}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* describe the Bookmark standard-setting method and build an item map at a
  response probability of 0.67;
* turn a cut on the $\theta$ scale into a raw-score cut;
* estimate classification accuracy and consistency at a cut score;
* report IRT results to people who do not use R, with a written summary, a
  report and a dashboard.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[cut score](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#cut-score),
[standard setting](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#standard-setting),
[response probability](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#response-probability),
[classification accuracy](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#classification-accuracy),
[classification consistency](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#classification-consistency),
[test characteristic curve](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#test-characteristic-curve).

## The ideas

A **cut score** divides a scale into categories such as *pass* and *fail*, or
*below basic*, *proficient* and *advanced*. Where the cut goes is a judgement
about what performance is good enough, made by people who know the content
and the consequences. **Standard setting** is the family of structured
procedures for making that judgement defensibly [@cizek2007].

The **Bookmark method** is closely tied to IRT. Items are ordered from
easiest to hardest in an *ordered item booklet*, where each item's location
is the $\theta$ at which a test taker has a fixed probability (usually 0.67,
the **response probability** RP67) of answering it correctly. Each panelist
places a bookmark after the last item that a *just-qualified* candidate
should master. The location of the bookmarked item is that panelist's cut,
and the panel's cut is usually the median over panelists after several
rounds of discussion. For a 2PL item, the RP67 location is

$$\theta_{0.67} = b + \frac{\ln(0.67/0.33)}{a}.$$

Once a cut is fixed on the $\theta$ scale, two numbers describe how well the
test sorts people. **Classification accuracy** is the proportion of people
whose estimated category matches their true category. **Classification
consistency** is the proportion who would be placed in the same category on
two independent administrations of the test. Both can be estimated from a
single administration using the scores and their standard errors
[@rudner2001].

Finally, results have to be communicated. People who make decisions with test
scores rarely read item parameters. They need a short, honest summary of what
the test measures, how precisely, for whom it works, and what the scores mean.

## Example 1: Setting a proficiency standard

A provincial Grade 6 science test has 36 items. We simulate a calibration on
2,500 students.

```{r data-reporting-1}
# Simulated 36-item science test, 2,500 students.
set.seed(1212)
a <- matrix(rlnorm(36, 0.15, 0.25)); b <- sort(rnorm(36, 0, 1))
resp <- simdata(a, matrix(-a * b), N = 2500, itemtype = "2PL")
colnames(resp) <- sprintf("S%02d", 1:36)
```

```{r}
mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
pars <- coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
booklet <- data.frame(item = rownames(pars), a = pars[, "a"], b = pars[, "b"])
booklet$rp67 <- booklet$b + log(0.67 / 0.33) / booklet$a
booklet <- booklet[order(booklet$rp67), ]
booklet$page <- seq_len(nrow(booklet))
head(booklet, 8)
```

The ordered item booklet is `booklet`, one page per item. Suppose eight
panelists, after two rounds of discussion, place their bookmarks for
*proficient* on these pages:

```{r}
bookmarks <- c(20, 22, 21, 23, 22, 24, 21, 22)
panel_cuts <- booklet$rp67[bookmarks]
theta_cut <- median(panel_cuts)
c(theta_cut = theta_cut, spread = sd(panel_cuts))
```

The standard deviation of the panelists' cuts, divided by the square root of
the number of panelists, is a rough standard error of the panel's cut. It
should be reported alongside the cut.

Teachers and parents see raw scores, so we convert the cut with the **test
characteristic curve**: The expected number correct at $\theta$.

```{r}
raw_cut <- expected.test(mod, matrix(theta_cut))
c(theta_cut = theta_cut, expected_raw = raw_cut, raw_cut = ceiling(raw_cut))
```

How many students are classified as proficient, and how accurately?

```{r}
sc <- fscores(mod, full.scores.SE = TRUE)
above <- sc[, 1] >= theta_cut
p_above <- pnorm((sc[, 1] - theta_cut) / sc[, 2])
c(percent_proficient = mean(above),
  accuracy = mean(ifelse(above, p_above, 1 - p_above)),
  consistency = mean(p_above^2 + (1 - p_above)^2))
```

Accuracy compares each student's category with where their true score
probably lies; consistency asks how often two independent testings would
agree (here approximated from each student's posterior probability of being
above the cut). Consistency is always the lower of the two, because both
testings carry error.

An item map makes the cut concrete for teachers: It shows which items a
just-proficient student is likely to answer correctly (the items below the
line). Printing the text of a few items on each side of the line is a good
way to describe what *proficient* means.

```{r item-map, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Item map of the ordered item booklet with the proficient cut score."}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(booklet, aes(page, rp67, colour = rp67 <= theta_cut)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = theta_cut, colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = theta_cut + 0.15, label = "Proficient cut",
           colour = "#C0392B", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#2C5F8A", `FALSE` = "grey60"),
                      labels = c(`TRUE` = "mastered at the cut", `FALSE` = "not yet")) +
  labs(x = "Page in the ordered item booklet", y = "RP67 location (theta)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_mirtverse()
```

In a real programme, `item_map()` and `set_cuts()` in the [assessment
pipeline](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/assessment-pipeline.html#stage-8)
produce the booklet, record the panel's judgements, and report impact and
classification statistics for several cuts at once.

## Example 2: Telling the story

We return to the attitude scale from Chapter \@ref(polytomous) to show the
reporting tools on a different kind of instrument.

```{r data-reporting-2}
# Four 4-category attitude items (scored 1-4), 392 respondents.
resp <- Science
```

`select_model()` and `interpret()` give a plain-language summary that is a
good first draft for the methods and results sections of a report:

```{r}
sel <- select_model(resp, verbose = FALSE)
interpret(sel$best)
```

Read it critically before you use it: It flags the poor absolute fit and the
low precision, and a careful report says what that means for the intended
use of the scores.

`interpret_prompt()` packages the same results into a prompt you can paste
into an AI assistant to draft a longer narrative. Nothing is sent anywhere.

For people who want to see everything, mirtverse writes a complete HTML
report in one call, with the model comparison, the interpretation, tables,
figures, a sum-score conversion table, item health cards and the code to
reproduce it:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mv_report(sel, file = "science-attitudes-report.html")
```

For people who want to explore, a dashboard lets them move an ability slider,
click through items and download tables, without R:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mv_dashboard(sel$best, title = "Attitudes to science")
export_dashboard(sel$best, "science-dashboard.html", format = "html")
```

See [Sharing results with a
dashboard](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/dashboards.html) for
the options.

### A one-page memo

Decision makers usually want one page. A structure that works:

1. **The question.** What decision will the scores support?
2. **The answer.** One or two sentences: Can the test support it?
3. **The evidence.** Three to five bullets: Precision where the decision is
   made, classification accuracy, fairness checks, any items removed.
4. **What it means.** The consequences of the cut for the people tested,
   for example the percentage classified in each category and how many are
   close to the cut.
5. **Recommendations and limits.**

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. In Example 1, how many raw-score points does the cut move if every
   panelist moves their bookmark one page later?
2. Repeat the item map with RP50 instead of RP67. Does the cut move up or
   down? Why does the choice of response probability matter to panelists?
3. Add a second cut for *advanced* at page 30. Estimate the accuracy of the
   three-category classification.
4. Write the "answer" and "evidence" parts of a memo about the proficiency
   cut in Example 1.
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
cut_later <- median(booklet$rp67[bookmarks + 1])
c(expected.test(mod, matrix(theta_cut)), expected.test(mod, matrix(cut_later)))

rp50 <- sort(booklet$b)
c(rp67_cut = theta_cut, rp50_cut = median(rp50[bookmarks]))

adv <- median(booklet$rp67[rep(30, 8)])
cats <- cut(sc[, 1], c(-Inf, theta_cut, adv, Inf), labels = c("below", "proficient", "advanced"))
p_cat <- cbind(pnorm((theta_cut - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2]),
               pnorm((adv - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2]) - pnorm((theta_cut - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2]),
               1 - pnorm((adv - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2]))
mean(p_cat[cbind(seq_len(nrow(p_cat)), as.integer(cats))])
```

1. Hardly at all here, because the items in that part of the booklet have
   very similar RP67 locations. Where the booklet has gaps between items, a
   single page can move the cut a lot, which is worth showing panelists.
2. With RP50 every item's location is lower, so the same bookmark gives a
   lower cut. Panelists must understand what "mastered" means (a 50% or a
   67% chance), or their bookmarks will not mean what they intend.
4. For example: "The test can support a proficient/not proficient
   decision. About 93% of students are expected to be classified correctly,
   and 89% would be classified the same way if tested again. The panel's
   eight judgements were close together, and about one student in five is
   classified as proficient." Use the numbers from your own output, and add
   the standard error at the cut (`1 / sqrt(testinfo(mod, matrix(theta_cut)))`).

</details>

<div class="lab">
The course map ends with a final project: A full analysis of a dataset of
the student's choice, handed in as an `mv_report()` or a dashboard plus a
two-page memo. The [assessment
pipeline](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/assessment-pipeline.html)
is a useful checklist for it.

## Further reading {-}

Cizek and Bunch [-@cizek2007] describe the Bookmark method and other
standard-setting procedures. Rudner [-@rudner2001] shows how to estimate
classification accuracy from IRT results. The *Standards* [@aera2014] set out
what to report about cut scores.
